beats.say: Even if your password is stolen, a second step can protect the account. This is called two-step verification.
The strongest are passkeys and security keys. They do not work on fake sites.
The code is only for you. Anyone asking for it, even as your bank, is a scammer.

messages.text: Do not share this code with anyone, not even bank staff.

beats.say: If approval requests you did not expect keep coming, someone is trying to sign in with your password.

checkpoint.prompt: What do you do with an unexpected request?

options.label: Approve it so it stops
options.feedback: If you approve, the attacker gets in.

options.label: Deny it and change my password
options.feedback: Right. Then tell IT security too.

scenes.title: Night requests
scenes.intro: It is two at night and you are asleep. Your phone keeps asking you to approve a sign-in.

steps.say: You are not signing in anywhere.

actions.label: Approve
actions.feedback: You are not signing in, so this is someone else. Approving lets the person with your password in.

actions.label: Deny
actions.feedback: Right. Always deny a request you did not expect.

actions.label: Approve so it stops
actions.feedback: Push bombing counts on exactly this: that you get tired and approve. Approving opens the account.

actions.label: Deny
actions.feedback: Right. Repeated requests mean someone knows your password.

actions.label: This is not me, report
actions.feedback: Great. Reporting shows the attack to the security team at once.

body.text: Hi, a night check is running. Approve the last request so your account is not blocked.

actions.label: OK, I will approve
actions.feedback: IT support never asks you to approve a request. This is the second half of the attack.

actions.label: Block and report
actions.feedback: Right. An unknown number writing at night is not support, it is the attacker.

steps.label: You opened the portal yourself
steps.say: Your password is stolen. What now?

actions.label: Change password now
actions.feedback: Right. Then tell the security team so they sign out all open sessions.

actions.label: I will look in the morning
actions.feedback: The attacker knows your password and will try again. Change it now.

question.prompt: Which second step resists phishing best?

options.label: SMS code
options.feedback: A fake site can ask for the code, and your SIM can be moved to someone else.

options.label: Authenticator app
options.feedback: Better than SMS, but you can still type the code into a fake site.

options.label: Passkey or security key
options.feedback: Right. A key only works with the genuine site.

options.label: Code sent by email
options.feedback: If your email is taken over, so is the code.

scenes.explain: Any second step is better than a password alone. Choose a key when you can.

scenes.prompt: Find the danger in these messages.

body.text: Hi Aynur! It is Nigar, this is my new number.
I sent a code to your number by mistake.
Please send me the six-digit code you just got.
Hurry, it expires in two minutes.

spots.label: Unknown number
spots.explain: A familiar name, but a new number. Call your friend's old number to check.

spots.label: "Sent by mistake"
spots.explain: A code does not reach your number by mistake. Someone is trying to get into your account.

spots.label: Code request
spots.explain: If you give this code, the scammer takes over your account and writes to your friends as you.

spots.label: Rush
spots.explain: Little time leaves no room to think. Never send a code to anyone.

scenes.prompt: Put the steps to set up an authenticator app in order.

items.label: Turn on two-step verification in your account settings
Scan the QR code on screen with the app
Enter the code the app shows
Keep the backup codes somewhere safe

scenes.explain: Backup codes help you get back in if you lose your phone.

points: When you can, choose a passkey or an authenticator app.
Never tell or send a code to anyone.
Deny unexpected requests, change your password, report.
